Although the NAACP had several legal victories against segregation in graduate schools and universities, those did not affect elementary and secondary public schools. So the organization next turned its focus to K–12 schools. Read the following passage about
, the most important legal win for the NAACP. Then answer the question below.
In the early 1950s, about forty percent of students attended segregated public schools, mostly but not always in the South. The 1896
Supreme Court decision allowed states to create "separate but equal" schools for African American students, but Black families argued that their schools were underfunded and inferior.

textContent.text: With NAACP support, families in several states filed lawsuits against their local school districts to challenge school segregation. One plaintiff, Oliver Brown, filed a lawsuit because his eight-year-old daughter, Linda, had to attend a Black school twenty-one blocks away from their house rather than a white school just seven blocks away. Brown's lawsuit was combined with four others when it was considered by the Supreme Court.

The court decided in 1954 that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. The decision emphasized that even if segregated schools had equal "tangible" factors, such as buildings, financial support, and qualified teachers, they created a feeling of social inferiority among African American students that "may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone." Therefore, the Court argued that segregated schools could never be equal, as required by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Although the NAACP had several legal victories against segregation in graduate schools and universities, those did not affect elementary and secondary public schools. So the organization next turned its focus to K–12 schools. Read the following passage about
, the most important legal win for the NAACP. Then follow the instructions below.
In the early 1950s, about forty percent of students attended segregated public schools, mostly but not always in the South. The 1896
Supreme Court decision allowed states to create "separate but equal" schools for African American students, but Black families argued that their schools were underfunded and inferior.

textContent.text: With NAACP support, families in several states filed lawsuits against their local school districts to challenge school segregation. One plaintiff, Oliver Brown, filed a lawsuit because his eight-year-old daughter, Linda, had to attend a Black school twenty-one blocks away from their house rather than a white school just seven blocks away. Brown's lawsuit was combined with four others when it was considered by the Supreme Court.

The court decided in 1954 that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. The decision emphasized that even if segregated schools had equal "tangible" factors, such as buildings, financial support, and qualified teachers, they created a feeling of social inferiority among African American students that "may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone." Therefore, the Court argued that segregated schools could never be equal, as required by the Fourteenth Amendment.

textContent.text: With NAACP support, families in several states filed lawsuits against their local school districts to challenge school segregation. The court decided in 1954 that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. Therefore, the Court argued that segregated schools could never be equal, as required by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Black and white civil rights activists were often targeted by a white supremacist group called the Ku Klux Klan (KKK). Read about the KKK. Then answer the question below.

This version of the KKK supported the idea that white Protestants were the only true Americans. It used public marches and violence to intimidate racial and religious minorities.

contents.text: While visiting family in Mississippi in August 1955, a 14-year-old Black boy from Chicago named Emmett Till was accused of flirting with an older white woman. He was kidnapped, beaten, and shot before his body was thrown in a nearby river. Two white men were tried for Till's murder but were found not guilty by an all-white jury. Read the responses to Till's death. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: Civil rights activists Dorie Ann Ladner and Joyce Ladner, who were young teenagers in Mississippi in 1955, were interviewed in 2011 about their activism.

Dorie Ann Ladner: Emmett Till…that's when a light bulb went off. Why aren't [his killers] being punished? That's when I went on my quest to try to understand the whole legal system and equal rights and justice under the law.…

Joyce Ladner: It was like a clarion call for action and that when we got older we were going to [respond to] his death. I mean, I can remember feeling that so strongly. I remember clipping [the local newspaper] every time there was an article about the Emmett Till case and the trial, and I kept a scrapbook.
Professor Cleveland Sellers from South Carolina, who was 11 years old in 1955, was interviewed in 2013 about the effect of Emmett Till's murder on his life and career.

Well, I was devastated by the fact that Emmett could have been me or any other black kid around that same age. And so, I related to that very quickly.…I had a [magazine with a photo of Till's body and] took it to school. Some other students had the same thing. And so, we had rational discussions about it. And, you know, the question comes up: How do you address that?

And I think, for us, it…would be our destiny to try to find remedies to a society that would allow that to happen, would condone that, and would actually free those who were responsible for that murder. And I think that that was a way in which we actually got away from revenge and hatred and those kinds of things. We talked about how we were going to use Emmett Till to build on, that we would rectify in our work and in our effort the dastardly tragedy that happened to Emmett Till.

contents.text: Based on the excerpts above, how did future civil rights activists respond to Till's murder?

choices.text: They were inspired to challenge racial violence and question the justice system.
They decided to leave the South and move to other areas of the country.
They decided white supremacy could only be fought with violence.
They learned to avoid white people in their communities.

CORE was founded in Chicago, Illinois, in 1942. It emerged from an organization of Christian

, meaning people who oppose violence, who wanted to use nonviolent techniques in the struggle for racial justice. CORE was particularly inspired by Mohandas Gandhi, an Indian lawyer and activist who used nonviolent techniques to challenge British rule in India.

textContent.text: CORE's early accomplishments included a 1942 sit-in that successfully desegregated a Chicago restaurant. They followed this with sit-ins in several cities around the country. In 1947, CORE organized an interracial bus trip around the Upper South called the Journey of Reconciliation. They wanted to test whether Southern states were following a recent Supreme Court ruling that said public transportation between states must not be segregated. Their trip drew attention to CORE and its use of nonviolent direct-action techniques, but buses continued to be segregated in the South.

In addition to CORE, another major center for nonviolent direct action was the Highlander Folk School. Founded in Tennessee in 1932, it helped poor and working adults in the region by offering classes on citizenship and political organizing. As it was one of the few racially integrated organizations at the time, its programs became a training ground for civil rights activists in later decades.

Professor Cleveland Sellers from South Carolina, who was 11 years old in 1955, was interviewed in 2013 about the effect of Emmett Till's murder on his life and career.

Well, I was devastated by the fact that Emmett could have been me or any other black kid around that same age. Joyce Ladner: It was like a clarion call for action and that when we got older we were going to [respond to] his death. I mean, I can remember feeling that so strongly. subheader.text: Who was Martin Luther King Jr.?

pieces.text: King was a pastor and civil rights leader who became nationally known during the Montgomery Bus Boycott. He went on to lead the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), a civil rights organization that promoted nonviolent direct action and participated in strikes, marches, and boycotts across the country. King is best known for his 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech during the March on Washington

He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 for his efforts toward racial justice for African American people. King was assassinated in 1968 while helping organize a strike of sanitation workers in Memphis, Tennessee. He was 39 years old.

subheader.text: What were conditions like for African American people in Birmingham?

subpoints.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, African American people in Birmingham were treated as second-class citizens and frequently subjected to violent attacks. Segregation laws affected all parts of life, making it illegal for Black and white people to share housing or space in restaurants, concert halls, or bus stations. During the civil rights movement, the Birmingham police attacked civil rights activists, and activists' homes were sometimes bombed by the Ku Klux Klan (KKK).

textContent.text: I think I should indicate why I am here in Birmingham, since you have been influenced by the view which argues against "outsiders coming in." I have the honor of serving as president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, an organization operating in every southern state, with headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia.…Several months ago the affiliate here in Birmingham asked us to be on call to engage in a nonviolent direct action program if such were deemed necessary. We readily consented, and when the hour came we lived up to our promise. So I, along with several members of my staff, am here because I was invited here.…

pieces.text: But more basically, I am in Birmingham because injustice is here.…Moreover, I am

of the interrelatedness of all communities and states. I cannot sit idly by in Atlanta and not be concerned about what happens in Birmingham. Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny. Whatever affects one directly, affects all indirectly. Never again can we afford to live with the narrow, provincial "outside agitator" idea. Anyone who lives inside the United States can never be considered an outsider anywhere within its bounds.

contents.text: King was criticized by the clergy for using direct action instead of negotiating more with city leaders. In response, he wrote about direct action and its effects. Read the following excerpt. Then answer the question.

textContent.text: You may well ask: "Why direct action? Why sit ins, marches and so forth? Isn't negotiation a better path?" You are quite right in calling for negotiation. Indeed, this is the very purpose of direct action. Nonviolent direct action seeks to create such a crisis and foster such a tension that a community which has constantly refused to negotiate is forced to confront the issue. It seeks so to dramatize the issue that it can no longer be ignored. My citing the creation of tension as part of the work of the nonviolent resister may sound rather shocking. But I must confess that I am not afraid of the word "tension." I have earnestly opposed violent tension, but there is a type of constructive, nonviolent tension which is necessary for growth.…The purpose of our direct action program is to create a situation so crisis packed that it will inevitably open the door to negotiation. I therefore concur with you in your call for negotiation. Too long has our beloved Southland been bogged down in a tragic effort to live in monologue rather than dialogue.

contents.text: King was criticized by the clergy for using direct action instead of negotiating more with city leaders. In response, he wrote about direct action and its effects. Read the following excerpt. Then answer the question.

textContent.text: You may well ask: "Why direct action? Why sit ins, marches and so forth? Isn't negotiation a better path?" You are quite right in calling for negotiation. Indeed, this is the very purpose of direct action. Nonviolent direct action seeks to create such a crisis and foster such a tension that a community which has constantly refused to negotiate is forced to confront the issue. It seeks so to dramatize the issue that it can no longer be ignored. My citing the creation of tension as part of the work of the nonviolent resister may sound rather shocking. But I must confess that I am not afraid of the word "tension." I have earnestly opposed violent tension, but there is a type of constructive, nonviolent tension which is necessary for growth.…The purpose of our direct action program is to create a situation so crisis packed that it will inevitably open the door to negotiation. I therefore concur with you in your call for negotiation. Too long has our beloved Southland been bogged down in a tragic effort to live in monologue rather than dialogue.

subheader.text: What were conditions like for African American people in Birmingham?

subpoints.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, African American people in Birmingham were treated as second-class citizens and frequently subjected to violent attacks. Segregation laws affected all parts of life, making it illegal for Black and white people to share housing or space in restaurants, concert halls, or bus stations. During the civil rights movement, the Birmingham police attacked civil rights activists, and activists' homes were sometimes bombed by the Ku Klux Klan (KKK).
